title: His first bass solo on Tantalizing a Cuban
summary: Soloing was hard; small combos later forced him to solo.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: When did he come into the band? Was that about --
Alvin Burroughs? About '36.
About '36 when he came in. You know, that 'Tantalizing a Cuban' --
Oh, right.
One of the few bass solos you get on those recordings.
Yeah.
Double time.
Yeah, that's the first bass solo I ever tried on a string bass.
Really?
Uh-huh.
You always -- never felt the urge to solo on bass, you were always a section man?
String bass, no.
Just play the time and --
Well, it always seemed -- string bass
is funny to me. It was all right, I could -- you know, play my four beats and my two beat, or whatever it is. I could swing the band. But soloing was kind of rough.
How do you mean?

Well, getting over them strings, you know, and my different positions, and things. And that "Tantalizing Cuban" is the one that woke me up. That was made up almost, you might as well say, on the stage of the Powell Theater.
Really?
Uh-huh.
You mean it woke you up to the -- how to solo, or the possibilities?
Yeah, that I could solo on the string bass, yeah.
Now practically every tune has got a bass solo (inaudible).

Yeah. Well, one thing got me really into soloing, like those small combos. You had to take a solo. Like those -- like trios, quartets, five piece orchestras. See, because bass had to take a solo. Didn't have that many instruments. It was different with a big band. You had all them solo trumpet players and saxophone players and trombone players. Everybody, you know, was playing solos. You didn't need much -- the bass very seldom needed to come

in with solos.
But like when Walter Fuller organized
that small combo, then I had to start playing solos, because
we didn't have but four pieces when we first started.
